Chapter 2 Petrol price Written 26/05/2021: (Note: In the article, there is a known error where ARIMA(2,1,3) is chosen despite not having the lowest AIC. In addition, AICc may be more appropriate over AIC.) This article uses an ARIMA time series model for weekly petrol price data over a period of about 13 years. knitr::opts_chunk$set(warning = FALSE) # Suppress warnings 2.1 Exploratory data analysis petrol.data <- read.csv("data/petrol.csv",stringsAsFactors=TRUE, header=F) iterations.max = 300 library(fpp3) n = length(petrol.data[,1]) petrolorig <- tsibble( Week = 1:n, Cost = ts(petrol.data[,1]), index = Week ) petrol <- tsibble( Week = yearweek(1:n), Cost = ts(petrol.data[,1]), index = Week ) petrolorig %>% autoplot() + labs(title = "Weekly Petrol Prices") + xlab("Week") + ylab("Petrol Price") ## Plot variable not specified, automatically selected `.vars = ## Cost` # zoom in # petrolorig %>% # slice(1:32) %>% autoplot() Figure 1 – Plot of weekly petrol prices series In Figure 1, non-constant variance is present as the variance in the period between about week 450 to week 625 seems larger than the rest of the data, particularly the period shortly after week 600. There is an upwards linear trend in the data, which a slow exponentially-decaying sample ACF plot would easily confirm. There are no obvious cycles or seasonality. Seasonality is not clearly present even if we zoom in on the plot for a small number of weeks. In any case, even if we wanted to model seasonality for weekly data, the fact that there is a (large) non-integer amount of weeks in a year (52.2) is problematic. 2.2 Converting to a stationary series We will apply a mathematical transformation and first differencing to adjust for heteroskedasticity and the linear trend respectively. The fable package suggests that a Box-Cox transformation with \(\lambda = -0.71\) is reasonable according to the guerrero feature. For simplicity, we will use \(\lambda = -1\) instead. Let \(y_t\) be the original series, then the transformed series (after a mathematical transformation and first differencing), is given by \[z_t = -(y_t^{-1} - y_{t-1}^{-1}).\] petrol %>% features(Cost, guerrero) ## # A tibble: 1 × 1 ## lambda_guerrero ## <dbl> ## 1 -0.493 lambda <- petrol %>% features(Cost, guerrero) %>% pull(lambda_guerrero) lvalue = round(lambda) petrolchanged <- petrol %>% mutate(Cost = box_cox(Cost, lambda)) # second plot petroldifftransf <- tsibble( #Week = yearweek(1:(n-1)), Week = (1:(n-1)), Cost = diff(ts(petrolchanged$Cost)), index = Week ) petroldifftransf %>% autoplot() + labs(title = "Transformed Weekly Petrol Prices") + xlab("Week") + ylab("Transformed Petrol Price") ## Plot variable not specified, automatically selected `.vars = ## Cost` Figure 2 – Plot of transformed weekly petrol prices series In Figure 2, we can see that the transformed series looks fairly stationary with little trend and the Box-Cox transformation has been helpful in adjusting for the non-constant variance. 2.3 Selecting appropriate ARIMA model z = ts(petrolchanged$Cost) tseries::adf.test(diff(z)[-1],k=0) # stationary ## ## Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test ## ## data: diff(z)[-1] ## Dickey-Fuller = -13.445, Lag order = 0, p-value = 0.01 ## alternative hypothesis: stationary petrol %>% model(mod = ARIMA(box_cox(Cost,lvalue))) %>% report() ## Series: Cost ## Model: ARIMA(1,1,1) ## Transformation: box_cox(Cost, lvalue) ## ## Coefficients: ## ar1 ma1 ## 0.7168 -0.2103 ## s.e. 0.0428 0.0597 ## ## sigma^2 estimated as 0.0003335: log likelihood=1850.96 ## AIC=-3695.91 AICc=-3695.88 BIC=-3682.19 petrolchanged %>% gg_tsdisplay(difference(Cost), plot_type='partial') + labs(y="Seasonally differenced") Figure 3 – Plots of sample autocorrelation and sample partial autocorrelation The sample ACF and PACF plots in Figure 3 exceed the confidence interval boundaries are multiple points and give no particular indication that a pure AR or MA model would fit our transformed series. 2.4 Choose between models using AIC freq=52 petrol.ts = ts(petrolchanged$Cost,freq=freq) diffpetrol.new = diff(petrol.ts) p_max=3 q_max=3 aic = matrix(0,ncol=q_max+1,nrow=p_max+1) for (i in 0:p_max) { #previously started at 1 for (j in 0:q_max) { fitARMAmle=arima(diffpetrol.new,order=c(i,0,j),method='ML',optim.control = list(maxit=iterations.max)) aic[i+1,j+1]=AIC(fitARMAmle) } } result = which(aic == min(aic), arr.ind=TRUE) #result[1]-1 #result[2]-1 #min(aic) rownames(aic) = 0:3 colnames(aic) = 0:3 aic ## 0 1 2 3 ## 0 -3872.747 -4087.614 -4134.328 -4167.551 ## 1 -4182.046 -4187.773 -4185.781 -4192.133 ## 2 -4187.124 -4185.776 -4184.407 -4193.625 ## 3 -4187.073 -4186.247 -4193.785 -4191.757 If we use a loop across different ARIMA models (varying degrees of AR and MA, keeping the differencing level fixed) we find that the best model according to AIC is ARIMA(2,1,3), which agrees with the model found by the order found by fable’s automatic ARIMA() function. Hence, we choose this model. (It may be useful to consider other types of models at this point too, but this article will focus on ARIMA.) The final model after back-transforming is \[ y_t = \left( \frac{1}{y_{t-1}} + \underset{(0.22)}{1.35} \left( \frac{1}{y_{t-1}} - \frac{1}{y_{t-2}} \right) - \underset{(0.14)}{0.57} \left( \frac{1}{y_{t-2}} - \frac{1}{y_{t-3}} \right) - e_t + \underset{(0.22)}{0.81} e_{t-1} - \underset{(0.06)}{0.23} e_{t-2} - \underset{(0.07)}{0.11} e_{t-3} \right)^{-1}, \] where the numbers underneath are standard errors for the parameter estimates. Note that the estimate for \(\sigma^2\) is \(9.3 \times 10^{-5}\). 2.5 Diagnostic tests and assessing model adequacy An augmented Dickey-Fuller test on the transformed series gives a p-value of less than 0.01, indicating that the transformed series is probably stationary. Let us now perform a Ljung-Box test for the null hypothesis that the residuals after fitting the ARIMA model are white noise. s = 4 # choose based on frequency of data # e.g. monthly data s=12, quarterly s=4, weekly s=4 or 5 seasonality = TRUE # parameter if (seasonality) {lag1 = 2*s} else {lag1 = 10} T1 = length(petrolchanged$Cost); threshold = T1/5 if (lag1>threshold) {lag1 = round(threshold)} arimafit = petrol %>% model(mod = ARIMA(box_cox(Cost,lvalue))) dof1 = arimafit %>% coef() %>% dim() %>% first() augment(arimafit) %>% features(.innov, ljung_box, lag=lag1, dof=dof1) ## # A tibble: 1 × 3 ## .model lb_stat lb_pvalue ## <chr> <dbl> <dbl> ## 1 mod 14.6 0.0240 According to Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021), it is advisable to choose our lag to be \(\min(10, n/5 \approx 140) = 10\) for this test, where \(n\) is the number of observations in our time series. Hence, we choose our lag to be 10 and we have 5 degrees of freedom (for two AR parameters and 3 MA parameters). The resulting p-value is 0.542, well above any typical significance level such as 0.05. Therefore, we conclude that there is insufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis that the residuals after fitting the ARIMA(2,1,3) model are white noise. qplot(sample = .innov, data = augment(arimafit)) + stat_qq_line() + labs(title = "Quantile-Quantile Plot") + xlab("Gaussian Quantiles") + ylab("Residuals") + theme(aspect.ratio=1) Figure 4 – Quantile-Quantile Plot The inverse transformation followed by differencing seemed to produce a stationary time series. The Ljung-Box p-value suggested that ARIMA(2,1,3) was a good fit, while the Q-Q plot casts doubt on whether prediction intervals based on the normal distribution can be trusted. 2.6 References Hyndman, R.J., & Athanasopoulos, G. (2021). Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd ed.). Melbourne, Australia: OTexts.

Chapter 3 Chickenpox Time Series 3.1 Introduction Written 04 Nov 2011: Treatment of chickenpox (varicella) cases uses up significant economic resources in Hungary. The Hungarian authorities were interested in the past in determining whether widespread distribution of a chickenpox vaccine would be appropriate (Meszner, Molnar, Rampakakis, Yang, Kuter, & Lara, 2017). The data used for this project are 521 weekly Hungarian chickenpox case counts by county from 2005 to 2014 inclusive, with Budapest regarded as its own administrative region. This data were provided publicly by Rozemberczki, Scherer, Kiss, Sarkar, and Ferenci (2021) and downloaded from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (University of California, 2021). The decision to make vaccines publicly available was already approved in 2018 (“Hungary to provide chickenpox vaccine”, 2018). Nevertheless, the data set may still be able to provide additional insights. My research question is to study whether population density plays a role in the behaviour of the time series. I am interested in whether higher population density may result in a greater number of “super-spreader” events. One key factor will be seasonality in the data set, as it is thought that that colder seasons and the timing of the school year have a significant effect on chickenpox cases (Rozemberczki et al., 2021). This may have different effects in the regions of differing population density. A natural choice in answering this research question is to fit multiplicative seasonal ARIMA models to the chickenpox case numbers, as we can study both seasonality and the case-number dependence on previous values and forecast errors. We will do so for four chosen Hungarian regions. 3.2 Exploratory data analysis Administratively, Hungary is split up into its counties, while the capital city, Budapest, is given a separate designation. Budapest which has, by far, the highest population density in the data set, was an obvious choice to include in my study. Of the remaining data sets, I have chosen the counties with the highest, median and lowest population densities, which are Pest, Heves and Somogy respectively (Hungarian Central Statistical Office, 2019). On a technical note, I chose to aggregate the weekly data into monthly data. Weekly data is difficult to handle for many reasons, particularly since the seasonal period is not exactly 52 (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, 2021). plot1 <- function() {par(mfrow=c(1,1),mar=c(5.1,4.1,4.1,2.1),mgp=c(3,1,0),oma=c(0,0,0,0))} chickenpox = read.csv("data/hungary_chickenpox.csv",header=T,stringsAsFactors = F) library(fpp3) library(writexl) library(bayesforecast) ## Registered S3 methods overwritten by 'bayesforecast': ## method from ## autoplot.ts forecast ## forecast.ts forecast ## fortify.ts forecast ## print.garch tseries ## ## Attaching package: 'bayesforecast' ## The following objects are masked from 'package:fabletools': ## ## model, report ## The following objects are masked from 'package:base': ## ## beta, gamma library(forecast) ## ## Attaching package: 'forecast' ## The following objects are masked from 'package:bayesforecast': ## ## fourier, naive chickenpox$Date = as.Date(chickenpox$Date, "%d/%m/%Y") pox = chickenpox %>% as_tsibble(index = Date) season = 12; test = 12; itns = 2000 # convert to monthly data buda1 = pox %>% select(BUDAPEST) %>% index_by(Month = yearmonth(Date)) %>% summarise(Cases=sum(BUDAPEST)) # check for outliers buda1_decomp <- buda1 %>% fabletools::model(STL(Cases)) %>% components() buda1_decomp %>% filter(remainder < quantile(remainder, 0.25) - 4*IQR(remainder) | remainder > quantile(remainder, 0.75) + 4*IQR(remainder)) ## # A dable: 0 x 7 [?] ## # Key: .model [0] ## # : Cases = trend + season_year + remainder ## # ℹ 7 variables: .model <chr>, Month <mth>, Cases <int>, ## # trend <dbl>, season_year <dbl>, remainder <dbl>, ## # season_adjust <dbl> bc.lambda.somogy <- somogy1 %>% features(Cases, guerrero) %>% pull(lambda_guerrero) plot.somogy = ts(as.numeric(somogy1$Cases),freq=season,start=2005) plot(plot.somogy,xaxt = "n",type='o',ylab="Somogy") dates = as.Date(somogy1$Month); sequence = attributes(plot.somogy)$tsp axis(1, at = seq(sequence[1], sequence[2], along = plot.somogy), labels = format(dates, "%Y-%m")) Figure 1 – Monthly chickenpox cases in Budapest, Pest, Heves, and Somogy from 2005 to 2014 Let us define an outlier as an observation that is either greater than 3 interquartile ranges above the 0.75 quantile, or 3 interquartile ranges below the 0.25 quantile, a fairly strict criteria detailed by Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021). The only observation that qualifies as an outlier under this criteria is the case number for January 2007 in the Heves series, which has a very clear peak in Figure 1. However, if we replace this observation with the average of the cases in January of the preceding and subsequent year, this outlier case disappears, but the very next month, February 2007 exceeds the outlier threshold value. Likewise, this behaviour repeats if we adjust the February 2007 observation. This process repeats itself until we replace the April 2007 observation, but then other observations at different times are flagged. Hence, it can be regarded that these values may not be true outliers, such as a once-off super-spreader event. Therefore, no change is made to the Heves series. 3.3 Methodology 3.3.1 Initial setup This project will use R to fit Bayesian models (R Core Team, 2021). The interface used to write in R is RStudio (RStudio Team, 2021). The Stan programming language is indirectly used (Carpenter et al., 2017). Please see Appendices 1 and 2 for R packages used and R code respectively. The aggregation into monthly data was done computationally using the fpp3 package in R, which automatically loads some packages in the tidyverse collection of packages (Hyndman, 2021). This reduces the number of observations to 120 months’ worth of case counts, of which we will take 108 as training data and 12 as test data. Finally, as discussed in Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021), fpp3 is used to determine the value for \(\lambda\) in a Box-Cox transformation, in order to adjust for heteroskedasticity in the time series. Assuming the untransformed monthly series is \((x_t)\), this transformation is achieved for non-zero \(\lambda\) via the formula \(y_t = (x_t^\lambda - 1)/\lambda\). Central to our methodology is the R package bayesforecast, which interfaces with the programming language Stan, to fit Bayesian time series models (Alonzo & Cruz, 2020). 3.3.2 Order selection bayesforecast used for ARIMA order selection, the algorithm for which is described below. Note that the process compares the BIC of frequentist fittings to find the preferred order. Firstly, the following constraints are made for a multiplicative seasonal ARIMA model \[ y_t \sim SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_{12} \] \(p + q + P + Q \leq 6\) \(d + D \leq 2\) \(0 \leq p \leq 5, 0 \leq d \leq 2, 0 \leq q \leq 5\) \(0 \leq P \leq 2, 0 \leq D \leq 2, 0 \leq Q \leq 2\) Steps for model selection, with exhaustive search and approximations off (stepwise=FALSE,approximation=FALSE), are based on the algorithm by Hyndman and Khandakar (2008). The first two steps are used to ensure stationarity. Use Kwiatkowski–Phillips–Schmidt–Shin test(s) to determine \(d\). Use the period of an STL decomposition to determine \(D\). Exhaustively check the BIC of all possible models within the constraints to determine the preferred \({p,d,q,P,D,Q}\). 3.3.3 Prior and posterior distributions 3.3.3.1 Sampling model As previously, take \((x_t)\) as the untransformed monthly series. After the Box-Cox transformation, we have \(y_t = (x_t^\lambda - 1)/\lambda\). We can determine from our fittings in Section 2.2 that the maximum order of coefficients for the models we need to fit for our sampling model is \[y_t | \boldsymbol{\gamma} \sim \text{SARIMA}(1,0,2)(2,1,2)_{12}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\) represents the parameters of the model. Hence, we can simply determine the posterior distribution assuming this model, but all of the fitted models will have lower order coefficients than this one. Our sampling model is equivalently expressed as described below. \[ (1-\phi B)(1-\Phi_1 B^{12}-\Phi_2 B^{24})(1-B^{12})(y_t-\mu) = (1+\theta_1 B+\theta_2 B^2)(1+\Theta_1 B^{12}+\Theta_2 B^{24})\epsilon_t \] Therefore, \[ \begin{aligned} y_t ={}& \mu + \epsilon_t + \theta_1\epsilon_{t-1} + \theta_2\epsilon_{t-2} + \Theta_1\epsilon_{t-12} + \theta_1\Theta_1\epsilon_{t-13} + \theta_2\Theta_1\epsilon_{t-14} + \Theta_2\epsilon_{t-24} + \theta_1\Theta_2\epsilon_{t-25} \\ &+ \theta_2\Theta_2\epsilon_{t-26} + \phi(y_{t-1}-\mu) + (1+\Phi_1)(y_{t-12}-\mu) - (\phi+\phi\Phi_1)(y_{t-13}-\mu) \\ &+ (\Phi_2-\Phi_1)(y_{t-24}-\mu) + (\phi\Phi_1-\phi\Phi_2)(y_{t-25}-\mu) - \Phi_2(y_{t-36}-\mu) \\ &+ \phi\Phi_2(y_{t-37}-\mu), \quad \epsilon_t \mid \sigma \sim N(0, sd=\sigma). \end{aligned} \] (Equation 1) Take \(\epsilon_{11} = \cdots = \epsilon_{36} = 0\). Hence, the likelihood for our sampling model is given by \[ \begin{aligned} y_t \mid \{&\mu, \sigma, \phi, \Phi_1, \Phi_2, \theta_1, \theta_2, \Theta_1, \Theta_2, \epsilon_t, \epsilon_{t-1}, \epsilon_{t-2}, \epsilon_{t-13}, \epsilon_{t-14}, \epsilon_{t-24}, \epsilon_{t-25}, \epsilon_{t-26}, \\ &y_{t-1}, y_{t-12}, y_{t-13}, y_{t-24}, y_{t-25}, y_{t-36}, y_{t-37}, y_1, \ldots, y_{36}\} \sim N(*, sd=\sigma) \end{aligned} \] where * is the expression on the right-hand side of Equation 1 and $t = 37, , 108. (In ARIMA models, the sampling model is assumed to be normal.) Define \[ \begin{aligned} \widehat{y}_t ={}& \mu + E[\epsilon_t] + \theta_1\epsilon_{t-1} + \theta_2\epsilon_{t-2} + \Theta_1\epsilon_{t-12} + \theta_1\Theta_1\epsilon_{t-13} + \theta_2\Theta_1\epsilon_{t-14} + \Theta_2\epsilon_{t-24} + \theta_1\Theta_2\epsilon_{t-25} \\ &+ \theta_2\Theta_2\epsilon_{t-26} + \phi(y_{t-1}-\mu) + (1+\Phi_1)(y_{t-12}-\mu) - (\phi+\phi\Phi_1)(y_{t-13}-\mu) \\ &+ (\Phi_2-\Phi_1)(y_{t-24}-\mu) + (\phi\Phi_1-\phi\Phi_2)(y_{t-25}-\mu) - \Phi_2(y_{t-36}-\mu) \\ &+ \phi\Phi_2(y_{t-37}-\mu) \\[1em] ={}& \mu + \theta_1\epsilon_{t-1} + \theta_2\epsilon_{t-2} + \Theta_1\epsilon_{t-12} + \theta_1\Theta_1\epsilon_{t-13} + \theta_2\Theta_1\epsilon_{t-14} + \Theta_2\epsilon_{t-24} + \theta_1\Theta_2\epsilon_{t-25} + \theta_2\Theta_2\epsilon_{t-26} \\ &+ \phi(y_{t-1}-\mu) + (1+\Phi_1)(y_{t-12}-\mu) - (\phi+\phi\Phi_1)(y_{t-13}-\mu) \\ &+ (\Phi_2-\Phi_1)(y_{t-24}-\mu) + (\phi\Phi_1-\phi\Phi_2)(y_{t-25}-\mu) - \Phi_2(y_{t-36}-\mu) \\ &+ \phi\Phi_2(y_{t-37}-\mu). \end{aligned} \] (Equation 2) At iteration \(t\) of our algorithm, we will generate \(\epsilon_t\) from \(\epsilon_t \mid \sigma \sim N(0, sd = \sigma)\) iid for \(t = 37, \ldots, 108\). However, for any iteration prior iteration \(n = 1, \ldots, t\) set \(\epsilon_n = y_n - \widehat{y}_n\), as defined in Equation 2.
